papers.title_in_file: Machine Learning meets Quantum Foundations: A Brief Survey
papers.version_note: arXiv:2003.11224v2 [quant-ph] 12 Jun 2020, dated June 15, 2020. The text layer ends with a blank 18th segment after the last page break; the paper has 17 pages.
papers.what_it_is: A survey of work at the interface of machine learning and quantum foundations (Bell nonlocality, state classification, hidden-variable neural networks), with background sections and open questions; it reports no new data.

existing.note: The value is right and complete. The sentence is on printed page 12 of the text layer (the Conclusion starts on p12 and the page-13 header comes after it), not p13 as the stored anchor says.
existing.anchor: Section IX Conclusion and Future Work, p12
quotes: In many of the applications, e.g. classification of entangled states, the computer gives a guess, but we are not sure about the correctness. This is never said and cannot be overlooked, as it is a limitation of these applications.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own statement of a limitation, not tested in the paper.

existing.note: The abstract says this word for word.
quotes: Recently, ideas from machine learning have successfully been applied to different problems in quantum foundations. Here, we compile the representative works done so far at the interface of machine learning and quantum foundations.
existing.certainty_reason: The authors' own claim; the survey cites the works and does not test them.

assertions.value: The authors state that the survey has eight sections after the introduction, and that works they could not cover in detail in the application sections are mentioned briefly in a later section.
assertions.anchor: Section I Introduction, p2
quotes: The survey includes eight sections excluding the introduction (section I).
We include such works brieﬂy in section VIII.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own structure and scope in Section I.

assertions.value: The authors state that data sharing is not applicable to the survey because no new data were created or analyzed in the study.
assertions.anchor: Data Availability, p13
quotes: Data sharing is not applicable to this survey as no new data were created or analyzed in this study.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states its own scope: it reports no new data.
assertions.reader_inference: Every performance claim in the survey is therefore cited from other work, not measured here.

assertions.value: The authors state that reinforcement learning and supervised learning have been used for determining the maximum quantum violation of various Bell inequalities, for classifying experimental statistics into local and nonlocal sets, for training AI to play Bell nonlocal games, for using hidden neurons as hidden variables to complete quantum theory, and for machine learning-assisted state classification.
assertions.anchor: Section I Introduction, p2
quotes: the methods from reinforcement learning and supervised learning have been used for determination of the maximum quantum violation of various Bell inequalities,

the classiﬁcation of experimental statistics in local/nonlocal sets, training AI for playing Bell nonlocal games, using hidden neurons as hidden variables for completion of quantum theory, and machine learning-assisted state classiﬁcation [51–54]
assertions.certainty_reason: A summary of cited work [51-54], not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors speculate that machine learning or artificial intelligence, presumably with some form of quantum computation, may capture somehow the essence of Bell nonlocality and contextuality, and they add that human abstraction and reasoning could be far more complicated than the capabilities of machines.
assertions.anchor: Section I Introduction, p2
quotes: machine learning or artiﬁcial intelligence, presumably with some form of quantum computation, may capture somehow the essence of Bell nonlocality and contextuality.
human abstraction and reasoning could be far more complicated than the capabilities of machines.
assertions.certainty_reason: An explicit speculation by the authors, with no evidence in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors quote Mitchell (1997) for the definition that a computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with E.
assertions.anchor: Section II Machine Learning, p2
quotes: According to Mitchel (1997) [56]
A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if the performance at tasks in T , as measured by P, improves with E.
assertions.certainty_reason: A definition the paper attributes to other work [56].

assertions.value: The authors state that, depending on the kind of experience the machine is permitted to have, machine learning algorithms can be categorized into supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.
assertions.anchor: Section II Machine Learning, p2
quotes: the machine learning algorithms can be categorized into supervised learning, unsupervised learning, and reinforcement learning.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own categorization, stated in Section II.

assertions.value: The authors state that the distinction between supervised and unsupervised learning can be blurry: by the chain rule of probability, learning P(x) can be turned into m supervised learning tasks, and learning P(y|x) can be turned into learning the joint distribution P(x, y).
assertions.anchor: Section II Machine Learning, Eq. 1 and Eq. 2, p3
quotes: the distinction between supervised and unsupervised learning can be blurry.
The above factorization (1) enables us to transform a unsupervised learning task of learning P (x) into m supervised learning tasks.
This last argument suggests that supervised and unsupervised learning are not entirely distinct.
assertions.certainty_reason: A short textbook argument stated in prose; the equations are not quoted in full.

assertions.value: The authors define under-fitting as the phenomenon where an algorithm fails to get sufficiently low training error, and over-fitting as the phenomenon where the training error is low but the test error is large.
assertions.anchor: Section II Machine Learning, p3
quotes: If a machine-learning algorithm fails to get sufﬁciently low training error; the phenomenon is called under-ﬁtting.
if the training error is low, but the test error is large, the phenomenon is called over-ﬁtting.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines both terms in Section II.

assertions.value: The authors illustrate with a figure that data sampled from a degree 3 polynomial with small noise is under-fitted by a degree 2 polynomial and over-fitted by a degree 30 polynomial.
assertions.anchor: Figure 1 caption, Section II, p3
quotes: Fitting data sampled from a degree 3 polynomial with small noise.
A degree 2 polynomial (orange dashed line) is under-ﬁtting
The degree 30 polynomial (red dashed-dotted line) is over-ﬁtting the data
assertions.certainty_reason: A schematic illustration of a textbook effect; the plot itself is not read.
assertions.reader_inference: This is a teaching illustration, not a result of the survey.

assertions.value: The authors state that restricted Boltzmann machines have been shown to be a good Ansatz to represent many-body wavefunctions, citing [59], and that the method has been applied to quantum many-body physics and quantum foundations problems.
assertions.anchor: Section II A Artificial Neural Networks, p3-4
quotes: RBMs have been shown to be a good Ansatz to represent many-body wavefunctions
This method has been successfully applied to quantum many-body physics and quantum foundations problems [54, 59].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work [54, 59].

assertions.value: The authors state that deep learning is a subset of machine learning, which can be thought of as a subset of AI.
assertions.anchor: Section II B Relation with Artificial Intelligence, p5, and Figure 4 caption
quotes: deep learning is a subset of machine learning which can be thought of as a subset of AI
Deep learning (DL) is a sub-discipline of machine learning (ML).
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper's own statement of how it uses the terms.
assertions.reader_inference: The text refers to Fig. 9 here, but the figure is Fig. 4; this is a cross-reference slip in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that quantum foundations seeks to understand and develop the mathematical and conceptual understanding of quantum theory, and that the survey focuses on entanglement, Bell nonlocality, contextuality and quantum steering.
assertions.anchor: Section III Quantum Foundations, p5
quotes: Quantum foundations seeks to understand and develop the mathematical as well as conceptual understanding
we will focus on non-classical features such as Entanglement, Bell nonlocality, contextuality and quantum steering in some detail.
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper states the scope of its quantum foundations coverage.

assertions.value: The authors define a bipartite pure state as entangled if it cannot be written as a product state, and an n-partite state as separable if it can be represented as a convex combination of product states.
assertions.anchor: Section III A Entanglement, Eq. 8, p5-6
quotes: is entangled if it cannot be written as a product state
ρsep is called separable if it can be represented as a convex combination of product states
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines both terms in Section III A.

assertions.value: The authors state that it is computationally not easy to check whether a mixed state, especially in higher dimensions and for more parties, is separable or entangled, and that for Hilbert space dimensions up to 6 the Peres-Horodecki (positive partial transpose) criterion can be used.
assertions.anchor: Section III A p6 and Section VI p11
quotes: Computationally it is not easy to check if a mixed state, especially in higher dimensions and for more parties, is separable or entangled.
For Hilbert space dimensions up to 6, one can use PeresHorodecki criterion
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement by the authors, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that there is no generic observable or entanglement witness for entanglement classification, as it is in fact an NP-hard problem [80], and that one must therefore rely on heuristic approaches.
assertions.anchor: Section VI Machine Learning-Assisted State Classification, p11
quotes: there is no generic observable or entanglement witness as it is in fact a NP-hard problem [80]. Thus, one must rely on heuristic approaches.
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work [80].

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [82-85], that for any entangled state rho there exists a Hermitian matrix W such that Tr(rho W) is less than 0 and Tr(rho W) is at least 0 for all separable states.
assertions.anchor: Section III A Entanglement, p6
quotes: for any entangled state ρ, there exists a Hermitian matrix W such that Tr(ρW ) < 0 and for all separable states ρsep, Tr(ρW ) ≥ 0 [82–85].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work [82-85].

assertions.value: The authors define a Bell experiment with N space-like separated parties, each with m inputs and each input corresponding to k outputs, as an (N, m, k) scenario, and state that the CHSH experiment is a (2, 2, 2) scenario and the simplest scenario in which Bell nonlocality can be demonstrated.
assertions.anchor: Section III B Bell Nonlocality, p6
quotes: A Bell experiment involving N space-like separated parties, each party having access to m inputs and each input corresponding to k outputs is referred to as (N, m, k) scenario.
experiment is a (2, 2, 2) scenario [101], and it is the simplest scenario in which Bell nonlocality can be demonstrated
assertions.certainty_reason: The paper defines the scenario notation in Section III B.

assertions.value: The authors state that the set of local behaviors forms a convex polytope whose facets are Bell inequalities, that the sets satisfy L within Q within NS (local, quantum, no-signalling), and that no-signalling behaviours outside Q are called post-quantum.
assertions.anchor: Section III B Bell Nonlocality, Figure 6, p6-7
quotes: The set of local behaviors (L ) forms a convex polytope, and the facets of this polytope are Bell inequalities
The no-signalling behaviours which do not lie in Q are also known as post-quantum behaviours.
assertions.certainty_reason: A background result stated without proof in the survey.

assertions.value: The authors state that all local hidden variable theories satisfy the CHSH inequality, that quantum behaviours can violate it up to the Tsirelson bound (printed in the text layer as "2 2", with the square root sign lost), and that the no-signalling bound on the CHSH inequality is 4.
assertions.anchor: Section III B Bell Nonlocality, Eq. 13, p7
quotes: All local hidden variable theories satisfy CHSH inequality.
Quantum behaviours achieve upto 2 2, known as the Tsirelson bound.
The upper bound for no-signalling behaviours (no-signalling bound) on the CHSH inequality is 4.
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement without proof in the survey.
assertions.reader_inference: The standard value of the Tsirelson bound is 2 times the square root of 2; the text layer lost the root sign.

assertions.value: The authors state, citing [102], that Kochen and Specker (as well as Bell) showed that non-contextuality conflicts with quantum theory, and that Kochen and Specker gave the first proof with a complicated construct involving 117 operators on a 3-dimensional space.
assertions.anchor: Section III C Contextuality, p7
quotes: It was shown by Simon Kochen and Ernst Specker (as well as John Bell) [102] that non-contextuality conﬂicts with quantum theory.
Kochen and Specker provided the ﬁrst proof of quantum contextuality with a complicated construct involving 117 operators on a 3-dimensional space [102].
assertions.certainty_reason: A result the paper attributes to other work [102].

assertions.value: The authors state that the Mermin-Peres square uses nine operators on a two-qubit system, each with eigenvalue plus or minus 1, and that there is no consistent way to pre-assign values to them, because each operator appears in exactly two lines (contexts) and one line has product minus the identity.
assertions.anchor: Section III C Contextuality, Figure 7, p7
quotes: There are nine operators, and each of them has eigenvalue ±1.
Notice that each operator (node) appears in exactly two lines or context.
assertions.certainty_reason: A known construction presented in outline in the survey.

assertions.value: The authors state that Bell nonlocality is regarded as a particular case of contextuality, where the space-like separation of the parties creates the context [104, 105].
assertions.anchor: Section III C Contextuality, p7
quotes: Bell nonlocality is regarded as a particular case of contextuality where the space-like separation of parties involved creates ”context” [104, 105].
assertions.certainty_reason: A statement the paper attributes to other work [104, 105].

assertions.value: The authors state that a state that manifests Bell nonlocality for suitably chosen measurement settings also exhibits steering, that a state that exhibits steering must be entangled, and that steering is asymmetric by definition.
assertions.anchor: Section III D Quantum Steering, p8
quotes: A state that manifests Bell nonlocality for some suitably chosen measurement settings also exhibits steering [130].
Furthermore, a state which exhibits steering must be entangled.
The concept of steering is asymmetric by deﬁnition
assertions.certainty_reason: Background results the survey states without proof.

assertions.value: The authors state that determining whether an assemblage admits a local hidden state model is a semidefinite program.
assertions.anchor: Section III D Quantum Steering, p8
quotes: Determining whether an assemblage admits LHS model is a semideﬁnite program (SDP).
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement without proof in the survey.

assertions.value: The authors state that characterizing the local set by Bell inequalities becomes intractable as the number of parties, settings and outcomes grows, and that for networks of independent sources the local set is remarkably non-convex, so proper analytical and numerical characterization is in general lacking.
assertions.anchor: Section IV Neural network as Oracle for Bell Nonlocality, p8
quotes: becomes intractable as the complexity of the underlying scenario grows
The local set is remarkably non-convex, and hence proper analytical and numerical characterization, in general, is lacking.
assertions.certainty_reason: The authors' motivation for the section, stated without proof.

assertions.value: The authors report that Canabarro et al. [52] use supervised machine learning with an ensemble of neural networks to tackle, via regression, the approximate version of the problem of deciding whether a behavior is classical or nonclassical; the label is the distance of the behavior from the local set, and the training points come from sampling non-signalling behaviors at random.
assertions.anchor: Section IV A Machine Learning Nonlocal Correlations, p8-9
quotes: Canabarro et al. [52] use supervised machine learning with an ensemble of neural networks to tackle the approximate version of the problem (i.e. with a small margin of error) via regression.
The training points are generated by sampling the set of non-signalling behaviors randomly and then calculating its distance from the local set via equation 18.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another paper's method [52]; the survey reports no accuracy figure.
assertions.reader_inference: The survey gives no numerical performance of the trained model.

assertions.value: The authors state that the distance predicted by the neural network is never equal to the actual distance, so there is always a small error, and that Canabarro et al. train the model for convex and non-convex scenarios and also for post-quantum correlations.
assertions.anchor: Section IV A, p9
quotes: Canabarro et al. [52] use supervised machine learning
the distance predicted by the neural network is never equal to the actual distance, i.e. there is always a small error
Canabarro et al. train the model for convex as well as nonconvex scenarios. They also train the model to learn postquantum correlations.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another paper's method and limits [52].

assertions.value: The authors report that Krivachy et al. [51] encode the causal structure into the topology of a neural network and numerically test whether the target distribution is learnable, treating a behavior as in the local set if it is learnable; for a network with adequate model capacity, a target distribution can be approximated if it is local.
assertions.anchor: Section IV B Oracle for Networks, p9
quotes: In reference [51], the authors encode the causal structure into the topology of a neural network
A behavior belongs to the local set if it is learnable.
For a neural network with adequate model capacity, a target distribution can be approximated if it is local.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another paper's method [51].
assertions.reader_inference: A target that is local but not learned to the required accuracy would look nonlocal; the survey does not discuss this false-positive risk.

assertions.value: The authors report that Krivachy et al. examined the triangle network with quaternary outcomes as a proof-of-principle example, that applying the technique to the elegant distribution suggests it is nonlocal as conjectured in [135], and that the distribution of Renou et al. appears to have nonlocal features for some parameter regime.
assertions.anchor: Section IV B Oracle for Networks, p9
quotes: The authors examine the triangle network with quaternary outcomes as a proof-of-principle example.
The application of the technique to the elegant distribution suggests that the distribution is
nonlocal as conjectured in [135].
appears to have nonlocal features for some parameter regime.
assertions.certainty_reason: Numerical findings of another paper [51], worded with 'suggests' and 'appears'.
assertions.reader_inference: The wording 'suggests' and 'appears' means these are numerical indications, not proofs of nonlocality.

assertions.value: The authors report that Dong-Ling Deng [54] uses the restricted Boltzmann machine architecture to detect quantum nonlocality in many-body systems, by treating a Bell inequality operator as a Hamiltonian whose ground state of the negative gives the maximal violation, and state that finding a ground state is QMA-hard in general.
assertions.anchor: Section V A Detecting Bell nonlocality with many-body states, p10
quotes: Dong-Ling Deng [54] employs machine learning techniques to detect quantum nonlocality in many-body systems using the restricted Boltzmann machine (RBM) architecture.
Finding the ground state of a quantum Hamiltonian is QMA-hard and thus in general difﬁcult.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another paper's method [54] and a background statement.
assertions.reader_inference: Section V A does not mention reinforcement learning for [54], but the Conclusion says [54] used RBM coupled with reinforcement learning; the survey is inconsistent on this point.

assertions.value: The authors state that DMRG, PEPS and MERA only work reliably for low-entanglement states, that DMRG works well only for systems with short-range interactions in the one-dimensional case, and that RBMs can represent quantum many-body problems beyond 1-D and low entanglement.
assertions.anchor: Section V A, p10
quotes: Moreover, DMRG works well only for systems with short-range interactions in the one-dimensional case.
RBM can represent quantum many-body problems beyond 1-D and lowentanglement.
assertions.certainty_reason: Background claims the paper attributes to other work [59].

assertions.value: The authors report that Bharti et al. [53], their own earlier work, turn the search for settings that violate a Bell inequality into a sequential decision process solved by reinforcement learning with proximal policy optimization, that the approach succeeds for well known convex Bell inequalities, and that it can also solve Bell inequalities corresponding to non-convex optimization problems such as in larger quantum networks.
assertions.anchor: Section V B Playing Bell Nonlocal Games, p10
quotes: the authors in Bharti et al. [53] have looked at a game-theoretic formulation of Bell inequalities
The authors transform this problem into a decision making process.
via proximal policy optimization - a state-of-the-art RL algorithm that combines two neural networks
The approach succeeds for well known convex Bell inequalities, but it can also solve Bell inequalities corresponding to non-convex optimization problems, such as in larger quantum networks.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of work [53] by the survey's own authors; no numbers are given in the survey.
assertions.reader_inference: The survey authors describe their own prior work and give no quantitative result for it.

assertions.value: The authors report that Bharti et al. [53] also present an approach to find settings for maximum quantum violation on near-term quantum computers, in which the state is a circuit of single-qubit rotations and CNOT gates on neighbouring qubits in a line, and the gates and measurement angles are optimized with a variational hybrid classical-quantum algorithm whose classical optimizer is reinforcement learning.
assertions.anchor: Section V B, p11
quotes: the authors in Bharti et al. [53] have looked at a game-theoretic formulation of Bell inequalities
The quantum state is parameterized by a circuit consisting of single-qubit rotations and CNOT gates acting on neighbouring qubits arranged in a linear fashion.
where the classical optimization is performed by RL.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of work [53] by the survey's own authors.

assertions.value: The authors state that if a state violates a Bell inequality it must be entangled, but that Bell inequalities cannot be used as a reliable tool for entanglement classification, since an entangled state might not violate one; Ma and Yung [141] therefore train a feed-forward neural network on the correlation vector of the CHSH inequality, and the authors report that its performance improved as model capacity was increased.
assertions.anchor: Section VI A Classification with Bell Inequalities, p11
quotes: In reference [141], the authors blend Bell inequalities with
If a state violates a Bell inequality, it must be entangled.
Bell inequalities cannot be used as a reliable tool for
The performance of the network improved as the model capacity was increased
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another paper's method and finding [141].
assertions.reader_inference: The text layer garbles the Werner-state example, so its thresholds are not entered.

assertions.value: The authors report that Harney et al. [143] modify restricted Boltzmann machines so that they can only represent K-separable states, by splitting the RBM into K partitions connected only within themselves, and that if training converges to a target state the state is K-separable, while if it does not converge the target is either of a different K-separable form or fully entangled.
assertions.anchor: Section VI B, p11
quotes: Harney et al. [143] use reinforcement learning with RBMs to detect entangled states.
This choice enforces a speciﬁc K-separable Ansatz of the wavefunction.
However, if the training does not converge, the Ansatz is insufﬁcient and the target state is either of a different K -separable form or fully entangled.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another paper's method [143].

assertions.value: The authors report that Lu et al. [144] detect entanglement with classic supervised learning and bootstrap aggregating, approximating the separable set by a convex hull, and show that accuracy improves when bootstrapping is combined with the convex hull approximation; and that Goes et al. [145] use automated machine learning to classify random two-qutrit states as separable, positive-partial-transpose entangled or negative-partial-transpose.
assertions.anchor: Section VI C Classification with Tomographic Data, p11-12
quotes: In Lu et al. [144], the authors detect entanglement
In a different approach Goes et al. [145]
The authors show that accuracy improves if bootstrapping of machine learning methods is combined with CHA.
classify random states of two qutrits as separable (SEP), entangled with positive partial transpose (PPTES) or entangled with negative partial transpose (NPT)
assertions.certainty_reason: Descriptions of other papers' methods and findings [144, 145]; no accuracy figure is given.

assertions.value: The authors report that Steven Weinstein [146] uses conditional restricted Boltzmann machines to give a completion of quantum theory that does not contradict Bell's theorem because the assumption of statistical independence is not respected, that with four hidden neurons the statistics predicted by the EPR experiment were reproduced with high accuracy, and that a conditional RBM is a more compact representation than an RBM.
assertions.anchor: Section VII Neural Networks as Hidden Variable Models, p12
quotes: Steven Weinstein provides a completion of quantum theory in reference [146].
doesn’t contradict Bell’s theorem as the assumption of “statistical independence” is not respected.
With four hidden neurons, the authors could reproduce the statistics predicted by EPR experiment with high accuracy.
This provides a more compact representation compared to an RBM.
assertions.certainty_reason: A description of another paper's construction and result [146].
assertions.reader_inference: The survey gives no accuracy figure for the 'high accuracy' claim.

assertions.value: The authors report that Krenn et al. [152] provide a computer program called Melvin that helps design novel quantum experiments, that its solutions were quite counter-intuitive and different from what a human scientist would ordinarily come up with, and that ideas from Melvin gave machine generated proofs of the Kochen-Specker theorem [159].
assertions.anchor: Section VIII A Few More Applications, p12
quotes: In reference [152], Krenn et. al. provide a computer program which helps designing novel quantum experiments.
Melvin provided solutions which were quite counter-intuitive and different than something a human scientist ordinarily would come up with.
The ideas from Melvin have further provided machine generated proofs of Kochen-Specker theorem [159].
assertions.certainty_reason: Results the paper attributes to other work [152, 159].

assertions.value: The authors state that the amalgamation of quantum theory and machine learning has led to a new area of research, namely quantum machine learning.
assertions.anchor: Section VIII A Few More Applications, p12
quotes: the amalgamation of quantum theory and machine learning has led to a new area of research, namely quantum machine learning [148].
assertions.certainty_reason: A background statement citing [148].

assertions.value: The authors state that designing experimental-friendly many-body Bell inequalities is a difficult task, and that it would be interesting if machine learning could help design optimal Bell inequalities for many-body systems, or if other representations such as convolutional neural networks could find optimal or near-optimal quantum values.
assertions.anchor: Section IX Conclusion and Future Work, p12
quotes: designing experimental-friendly many-body Bell inequalities is a difﬁcult task.
such as convolutional neural networks for ﬁnding optimal (or nearoptimal) quantum values.
assertions.certainty_reason: An open problem the authors state in the Conclusion.

assertions.value: The authors state, following [52], that it is an excellent idea to use anomaly detection for detecting non-classical behaviors, by training the machine with local behaviors only.
assertions.anchor: Section IX Conclusion and Future Work, p12
quotes: As mentioned in reference [52]
it is an excellent idea to deploy techniques like anomaly detection for the detection of non-classical behaviors.
This can be done by subjecting the machine to training with local behaviors only.
assertions.certainty_reason: A proposal by the authors, not tested in the paper.

assertions.value: The authors state that the intriguing open question is how the output of the computer can be employed to provide a certification of the result, and that probabilistic machine learning, including Bayesian optimization and automatic model discovery, could help.
assertions.anchor: Section IX Conclusion and Future Work, p12-13
quotes: The intriguing question is to understand how the output of the computer can be employed to provide a certiﬁcation of the result
One could use ideas from probabilistic machine learning in such cases [161].
assertions.certainty_reason: An open problem the authors state in the Conclusion.

assertions.value: The authors state that in [53] the agent gets a reward only at the end of each epoch, equal to the expectation value of the Bell operator, that such a reward scheme is sparse and might not be scalable, and that extending the approach to a multi-agent setting, with every space-like separated party a separate agent, would be exciting.
assertions.anchor: Section IX Conclusion and Future Work, p13
quotes: In reference [53], the authors used reinforcement learning to train AI to play Bell nonlocal games
Such a reward scheme is sparse and hence it might not be scalable.
It would be exciting to extend the approach to multi-agent setting where every spacelike separated party is considered a separate agent.
assertions.certainty_reason: A limitation and open problem the authors state in the Conclusion.
assertions.reader_inference: The scalability concern is stated for the survey authors' own method [53]; the survey does not test it.

assertions.value: The authors state that finding quantum Bell inequalities, the boundary separating the quantum set from the post-quantum set, is an interesting and challenging problem, and propose approximating them by supervised learning and opening the neural-network black box to guess physical principles.
assertions.anchor: Section IX Conclusion and Future Work, p13
quotes: Finding quantum Bell inequalities is an interesting and challenging problem.
it is interesting to see if it is possible to guess physical principles by merely opening the neural-network black box.
assertions.certainty_reason: An open problem the authors state in the Conclusion.

assertions.value: The authors state that, driven by the success of machine learning in Bell nonlocality, it is genuine to ask if the methods could solve problems in quantum steering and contextuality, and that it would be nice to see if techniques from the black-box approach to quantum theory could be connected to the Turing Test.
assertions.anchor: Section IX Conclusion and Future Work, p13
quotes: it is genuine to ask if the methods could be useful to solve problems in quantum steering and contextuality.
It would be nice to see if techniques from the black-box approach to quantum theory could be connected to TT.
assertions.certainty_reason: Open problems the authors state in the Conclusion.
assertions.reader_inference: The survey reports no result on steering or contextuality; these are stated as future directions only.
